title: The Last Well
premise: Felix Pemberton, a hospice nurse who has heard the dying count backwards for a decade, moves into Alder House to care for its last resident, Edith Vane. The house's mirrors begin lagging one second behind reality, and in that stolen second Felix sees figures: the six residents who vanished from Alder House in 1974, when Edith's husband sold their water rights and drained the town's last well. As the reflections grow bolder and the counting spreads to the living, Felix discovers she was born in that house and that her own mother was among the taken. To end it, she must return what was taken—the deed, the bones beneath the dry well, and her own buried name—before Edith signs the papers selling Alder House to developers. In the climax Felix descends into the well shaft as the mirrors close around her; she gives back her mother's name aloud, freeing the dead but forfeiting the identity 'Felix Pemberton,' which never truly existed. She survives as someone new, unnamed, watching Edith tear up the papers as the well fills with clean water.
about_author: Astrid Ishikawa is a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror about institutions, inheritance, and the things we agree not to notice. She lives near a reservoir and has never once looked at it after dark.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Felix Pemberton, POV. On her final shift at St. Ambrose Hospice, Felix hears Mr. Okafor count backwards from thirty and die exactly at zero, just like the others. Her supervisor offers her a lucrative live-in placement: Alder House, caring for its last resident. Felix accepts despite a cold dread she can't name. Beat: uneasy escape into a decision that feels like fate.

chapters.title: Alder House
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. She arrives at the decaying manor and meets Edith Vane, sharp-tongued and ninety-one, who mistakes Felix for someone called 'Mara.' A lawyer waits with sale papers Edith refuses to sign. That night Felix notices the hallway mirror holds her image a beat too long when she turns away. Beat: displacement and first wrongness.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Testing every mirror systematically, Felix confirms each reflection lags by exactly one second—and in that second, the reflected room contains six extra chairs at the dining table. Edith watches her measure and says only, 'You count too, don't you?' Beat: rational explanations begin to fail.

chapters.title: The Six Chairs
chapters.summary: Edith, POV (interleaved). Edith remembers 1974: her husband Gerald selling the town's water rights, the well sealed, six residents of Alder House gone within a month. She has spent fifty years signing nothing. In the present she warns Felix never to answer if the house calls her by another name. Beat: guilt preserved like a specimen.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Researching in the county archive, Felix finds the 1974 disappearances ruled accidental—a drowned child, a missing groundskeeper—but photos show six residents, all erased from records. One face stops her cold: a young woman wearing Felix's own locket. Beat: the past reaches forward and touches her.

chapters.title: The Locket
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Felix confronts the impossible locket in her jewelry box, engraved 'Mara' inside. Her adoption papers list Alder House as her birthplace. The mirror-Felix now moves independently during the lagged second, mouthing words. Beat: identity cracks open; the self she built is scaffolding over a hole.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Aren't
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Townspeople are warm until she mentions Alder House; then doors close. An old shopkeeper tells her the town still buys bottled water because 'the well remembers.' At home, the counting has started in the walls—backwards, patient, getting closer to zero each night. Beat: isolation deepens, dread becomes ambient.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Edith, POV. Edith admits Gerald didn't sell water rights—he stole them, poisoning dissenters and drowning the well to hide bodies. The six residents knew. Edith stayed silent, raised Mara's daughter elsewhere, and has refused to sign anything for fifty years because the signature would complete the transfer of guilt. Beat: complicity as slow poison.

chapters.title: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. The mirrors now lag two seconds, then three. In the stretched gap Felix sees the six residents living their final evening on loop: dinner, argument, descent to the cellar. When she tries to speak to them, they all turn to look at her at once. Beat: horror escalates from uncanny to active.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Following the loop's geography, Felix finds a bricked cellar door behind the pantry. Behind it, a shaft—the old well, dry for fifty years, breathing cold air upward. Scratched inside the brick: six names, and a seventh half-finished: MAR. Beat: the house's anatomy revealed; her name incomplete in stone.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. The counting in the walls reaches zero and begins again—from sixty, faster. Every clock in the house runs backwards overnight. Edith suffers a stroke and can no longer speak, but her eyes track Felix with urgent meaning toward the unsigned papers. Beat: time itself turns against the household.

chapters.title: The Lawyer Returns
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Mr. Halloway, the lawyer. Halloway arrives to force the signature, revealing he represents a development trust that has tried to buy Alder House every decade since 1974—and that his firm's founding partner was Gerald Vane's broker. He carries a pen that belonged to Gerald. Beat: the machinery of the original crime still running.

chapters.title: Reflections Argue Back
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Mirror-Felix speaks fully now during the lag: she is Mara, Felix's mother, kept in the glass since 1974. She explains the terms—the dead cannot leave until what was taken is returned, and the developers' purchase would seal them forever. Mara begs Felix to finish her name on the brick. Beat: ally and threat in one face.

chapters.title: The Deed Beneath
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Searching Gerald's study, Felix finds the original water-rights deed hidden under floorboards, signed in 1974 by coercion—six residents' signatures witnessed by fear. The document is the anchor binding them. Taking it triggers the house: every mirror shatters except one, which goes perfectly, horribly clear. Beat: theft of the theft; point of no return.

chapters.title: Halloway's Bargain
chapters.summary: Halloway, POV. Sensing the deed is found, Halloway offers Felix money and a clean identity to hand it over, revealing he knows she's Mara's daughter—his firm arranged her adoption. 'You were our contingency,' he says. Felix pretends to consider. Beat: justice outside the law takes shape as refusal.

chapters.title: The Vigil
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Felix keeps vigil over dying Edith, hearing her count backwards from ten across three days. Between counts, Edith surfaces enough to whisper: 'Not the paper. The water. Give it back to the ground.' Felix understands the deed alone won't suffice—the well must be unsealed. Beat: tenderness inside terror; instructions received.

chapters.title: Edith Vane, Zero
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Edith dies at zero, and for the first time the counting doesn't restart—it continues downward, negative numbers, wrong. The clear mirror shows Edith joining the six at the table, taking the seventh chair. Grief and relief war in Felix. Beat: death as both ending and recruitment.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Halloway, POV. With Edith dead, Halloway moves to probate-sign the sale himself. But the pen writes only backwards; the ink runs upward; every copy of the contract in his briefcase is blank. Outside, the town's taps run black. He drives to Alder House to retrieve the deed in person. Beat: institutional power meets something it can't invoice.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Breaking the brick, Felix climbs down the well shaft with the deed and a crowbar, following Mara's voice. The walls are lined with the six residents' remains and, at the bottom, the sealed cap Gerald poured. Above, Halloway's headlights sweep the drive. The lag between world and mirror is now minutes. Beat: claustrophobic descent toward reckoning.

chapters.title: The Last Well
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. At the shaft's bottom, Felix breaks the cap. Water rises—not flooding but rising to meet her, warm, tasting of iron and rain. She reads the six names aloud, then finishes the seventh: MARA. The dead step out of the mirrors into the water and dissolve upward like light in current. Beat: cathartic release; restitution made flesh.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Felix/Mara, POV blurring. Giving back the name costs Felix her history: her memories of being Felix Pemberton drain away like the water rising. She climbs out holding the deed, meets Halloway at the door, and hands him nothing but the sight of the well flowing again. His pen crumbles; he flees. She signs nothing. Beat: climax resolved through surrender, not victory.

chapters.title: Someone New
chapters.summary: Unnamed narrator, POV. Weeks later, a woman with no surname tends Alder House as its caretaker while the town's wells refill. Edith's estate, unsigned, passes to public trust; the house will become a hospice again. In the restored mirrors, reflections arrive exactly on time—except once a year, on the anniversary, when they arrive one second early, as if greeting her. Beat: quiet resolution; survival at the price of self, transformed into service.
